title: Paths by adding
hook: Counting routes across town sounds like listing them all. You only need to add.

knows: what a shortest route on a street grid is (only east or north)
doesNotKnow: that route counts add: each corner's count is the sum of the two before it
that these counts form Pascal's triangle

misconception: Counting routes means listing them all; the counts are too irregular to predict.
objective: The learner can explain that the number of shortest routes to a corner is the routes to the corner west of it plus the routes to the corner south of it, and use this to get 20 for a 3-by-3 grid.

claims.text: Every shortest route into a corner arrives from the corner to its west or the corner to its south, so its count is the sum of those two counts; along the edges there is 1 route (1 from one side plus 0 from the other).
claims.source: The last move of an east/north route is either east or north; the two sets of routes do not overlap. On an edge only one kind of move is possible. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 11): Last move is east or north, disjoint cases, so count = west + south; an edge corner has one predecessor.

claims.text: A 3-by-3 grid of blocks has 20 shortest corner-to-corner routes; the counts along the way are 1s on the edges, then 2, 3, 4, 6, 10 and 20.
claims.source: Grid of sums computed with node: rows 1 1 1 1 / 1 2 3 4 / 1 3 6 10 / 1 4 10 20; C(6,3) = 20; brute-force enumeration of 6-move strings with 3 easts also gives 20.

claims.text: Turned so Start is on top, the route counts are Pascal's triangle, where each entry is the sum of the two above it; 20 is the middle entry of row 6.
claims.source: Pascal's rule C(n,k) = C(n-1,k-1) + C(n-1,k); routes to (a,b) = C(a+b, a). E.g. Graham, Knuth and Patashnik, Concrete Mathematics, sec. 5.1. Row numbering starts at row 0 = 1.

claims.text: The 20 routes correspond to choosing which 3 of the 6 moves go east.
claims.source: Every shortest route is 3 easts and 3 norths in some order; C(6,3) = 20.

claims.text: A city 3 blocks east by 3 blocks north has 4 x 4 corners (the dots); 20 shortest routes go from one corner to the opposite one.
claims.source: Corners = (3 + 1)^2 = 16; routes = C(6, 3) = 20 (c2, c4). Question wording changed from '3-by-3 grid of blocks' to avoid confusion with the dots. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 11): (3+1)^2 = 16 corners; C(6,3) = 20 in node.

recall.question: On a street grid, 4 shortest routes reach the corner just west of yours and 6 reach the corner just south of it. How many reach yours (moving only east or north)?
recall.why: Every route into your corner comes from the west or from the south, so the counts add: 4 + 6 = 10.
